title: Pythagorean Theorem in 2D and 3D
short: Find missing lengths in plane figures and boxes.

blocks.html: Right angles are everywhere: walls meet floors, streets cross, edges of boxes meet. Wherever two perpendicular lengths are known, the Pythagorean theorem finds the distance across. When the answer is a square root, estimate it.

A ladder against a wall, a diagonal across a screen, a shortcut across a field: each is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs you know (or can measure). In a box, no single triangle reaches from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner, but two do: one across the floor, then one standing up on that floor diagonal.

Sketch the right triangle, label the legs and the hypotenuse, then use $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$. For the space diagonal of a box: first the floor diagonal $d^{2} = l^{2} + w^{2}$, then $D^{2} = d^{2} + h^{2}$.

blocks.name: g8-solid
blocks.cap: The dashed floor diagonal and the height make a right triangle whose hypotenuse (red) is the space diagonal.

blocks.title: A ladder
blocks.q: A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall with its foot 6 feet from the wall. How high does it reach?
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse: $6^{2} + h^{2} = 10^{2}$.

blocks.title: A screen
blocks.q: A screen is 16 inches wide and 9 inches tall. How long is its diagonal, to the nearest tenth of an inch?

blocks.title: A box
blocks.q: A box is 4 by 3 by 12 inches. How long is the longest rod that fits, from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner?

blocks.html: Using the theorem once in a box, or adding the three lengths. The space diagonal is not $4 + 3 + 12$; it takes two right triangles. (A shortcut: $D^{2} = l^{2} + w^{2} + h^{2}$.)
